title: How does JWT validation work — server checks signature (not tampered), checks expiration (exp claim), checks issuer (iss claim) — and why you should NEVER store sensitive data in the payload?
shortTitle: How JWT Validation Works and Why Never Store Sensitive Data in the Payload

s1_definition.profdef: JWT validation is the set of checks a server runs before trusting a token's claims. It verifies the signature against the expected key and algorithm (proving the token was not tampered with and really came from the issuer), checks the expiration claim exp (the token is not past its lifetime), checks the issuer claim iss and often the audience aud (the token was minted by and for the right parties), and may check not-before nbf and a revocation list. Only if every check passes does the server treat the claims as authoritative.
s1_definition.analogy: When a cheque arrives at National Bank of India, the clerk does several checks before paying: is the bank's signature genuine (signature check), is the cheque still within its validity date (expiry check), was it issued by our own bank and not a fake branch (issuer check). Only when all checks pass does the clerk pay out. And because the cheque's details are visible to anyone who holds it, the bank never prints a customer's PIN on it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Validate the signature, the expiry, and the issuer before you trust a single claim — and never write a secret on something everyone can read.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JWT validation is the set of checks a server runs before trusting a token's claims. It verifies the signature against the expected key and algorithm (proving the token was not tampered with and really came from the issuer), checks the expiration claim exp (the token is not past its lifetime), checks the issuer claim iss and often the audience aud (the token was minted by and for the right parties), and may check not-before nbf and a revocation list. Only if every check passes does the server treat the claims as authoritative.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a cheque arrives at National Bank of India, the clerk does several checks before paying: is the bank's signature genuine (signature check), is the cheque still within its validity date (expiry check), was it issued by our own bank and not a fake branch (issuer check). Only when all checks pass does the clerk pay out. And because the cheque's details are visible to anyone who holds it, the bank never prints a customer's PIN on it.

**One line to remember:** Validate the signature, the expiry, and the issuer before you trust a single claim — and never write a secret on something everyone can read.

sections.s2_technical:
Signature validation comes first. The server recomputes the signature over the header and payload using the configured key and the algorithm pinned by the server (not blindly trusting the header's alg, to avoid the "alg:none" and algorithm-confusion attacks). For example with jjwt: `Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).requireIssuer("national-bank").build().parseSignedClaims(token)` throws if the signature is invalid.

Expiry validation checks the exp claim against the current time, usually with a small clock-skew allowance. If `now > exp` the token is expired and rejected. Issuer and audience validation confirm `iss` equals your trusted issuer and `aud` includes your service, so a token minted for another system cannot be replayed against yours. For instance, `requireIssuer("national-bank")` and `require("aud","account-service")` enforce these. Many systems also check a jti against a revocation denylist for high-risk operations.

The senior point on sensitive data: the payload is only Base64Url-encoded, which anyone can decode. A JWT provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. If you store a balance, a PIN, a full card number, or personal identifiers in the payload, any party who captures the token — in a log, a browser history, a proxy — can read them. So the payload should carry only a subject identifier, roles or scopes, and timing claims. Anything sensitive must be fetched server-side after authorization, or, if it truly must travel, wrapped in JWE encryption.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India receives a token on every API call. Before honoring it, the Account Service must be certain the token was not altered, is still valid in time, and was issued by the bank's own auth server and not a counterfeit one. This is exactly what JWT validation does — signature, expiry, and issuer checks in sequence.

Problem 2 — A junior developer puts Rajesh's balance and PIN into the token to avoid a database lookup. A support engineer later pastes a failing request, token and all, into a ticket, and now the PIN is sitting in a ticketing system readable by many people. This is exactly why sensitive data must never live in the payload — the token is readable wherever it travels.

Our mini-project builds a `JwtValidator` that runs signature, expiry, and issuer checks and returns trusted claims. The demo validates a good token, rejects a tampered one, rejects an expired one, rejects a wrong-issuer one, and prints the decoded payload to prove it is readable.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four tokens — a good one, a tampered one, an expired one, and one from a fake issuer.

Step 1: The good token enters `validate`. The signature is recomputed over the header and payload and matches, so step one passes. The exp is in the future, so step two passes. The iss equals "national-bank", so step three passes. The trusted claims are returned.

Step 2: The tampered token (role changed to ADMIN, re-encoded, old signature kept) fails at step one because the recomputed signature no longer matches. It is rejected before any claim is trusted.

Step 3: The expired token has a valid signature, so step one passes, but step two finds now is past exp plus skew, so it is rejected.

Step 4: The wrong-issuer token passes signature and expiry but step three finds iss is "fake-bank", not "national-bank", so it is rejected. Finally the demo decodes the payload in plain sight, proving anyone can read it, which is why no secret may live there.

```text
2026-10-31 22:55:00.010 INFO    [JwtValidationDemo] Good token claims: {sub=rajesh, role=CUSTOMER, iss=national-bank}
2026-10-31 22:55:00.011 SEVERE  [JwtValidationDemo] Rejected tampered token: signature invalid (tampered)
2026-10-31 22:55:00.012 SEVERE  [JwtValidationDemo] Rejected expired token: token expired
2026-10-31 22:55:00.013 SEVERE  [JwtValidationDemo] Rejected wrong-issuer token: untrusted issuer: fake-bank
2026-10-31 22:55:00.014 WARNING [JwtValidationDemo] Payload is readable by anyone -> never store PIN/balance/card in it
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Incoming request: Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
    │
    ▼
  JwtValidator.validate(token)
    │
    ├─ 1. signature == recomputed? ──no──→ 401 (tampered)
    │              │ yes
    ├─ 2. now <= exp + skew? ────────no──→ 401 (expired)
    │              │ yes
    ├─ 3. iss == expected? ──────────no──→ 401 (untrusted issuer)
    │              │ yes
    ▼
  trusted claims {sub, role, iss} → authorization proceeds
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — JwtValidator ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │        JwtValidator          │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ - secret: String             │
  │ - expectedIssuer: String     │
  │ - clockSkewSeconds: long     │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + validate(token): Map       │  throws TokenValidationException
  │ + hmac(secret,data): String  │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Validation order (fail fast):
    1. signature  (integrity + authenticity)
    2. exp        (freshness, with clock skew)
    3. iss / aud  (right issuer, right audience)
    4. jti        (not revoked — optional denylist)

  Contract for validate(token):
    Post: returns trusted claims ONLY if all checks pass
    Security: pin server algorithm; never trust header "alg" blindly
    Rule: payload is readable → NEVER store PIN/balance/card/PII
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
JWT validation is the sequence of checks a server performs before it trusts any claim in a token. First it verifies the signature by recomputing it with the server's configured key and pinned algorithm, which proves the token was not tampered with and really came from the issuer. Then it checks the expiration claim exp against the current time with a small clock-skew allowance. Then it checks the issuer claim iss, and usually the audience aud, so a token minted elsewhere cannot be replayed against this service. Only when all of these pass are the claims treated as authoritative.

In my banking project every service runs this pipeline, and the gateway runs it too for defense in depth. In my demo a good token passes all three checks, a tampered token fails the signature check, an expired token fails the expiry check, and a token from a fake issuer fails the issuer check. I also pin the algorithm on the server rather than trusting the header's alg field, because blindly trusting it opens the alg-none and algorithm-confusion attacks.

The reason I never store sensitive data in the payload is that a JWT gives integrity and authenticity but not confidentiality. The payload is only Base64Url-encoded, so anyone who captures the token in a log, a proxy, or a browser history can decode and read every claim. If a balance, a PIN, or a card number were in there, it would leak the moment the token did.

So in a bank I keep the payload to a subject identifier, a role or scopes, and timing claims, and I fetch anything sensitive from the database only after authorization. For high-risk actions I also check a small revocation denylist by jti, and if a payload genuinely must be confidential I use JWE encryption rather than a plain signed token.

---

keyPoints: JWT: Header.Payload.Signature — Base64 encoded, not encrypted
Signature verifies integrity — payload is readable by anyone
Access token: short-lived (15 min). Refresh token: long-lived (days)
Store in HttpOnly cookie (XSS-safe), never in localStorage
